I am checking whether Q’s peer-scoring and nested cyclical-monotonicity results actually apply to P’s prompt-only reviewer–critic loop. I will look for a testable design or impossibility claim, with particular attention to what is verified, who controls the score, and whether the agents have the strategic type/utility assumptions Q needs.

The scan’s proposed derivation from nested cyclical monotonicity to AR disagreement is not licensed by Q. Q sec. 1.3 (around lines 522ff) characterizes direct single-agent report/action rules under known feasible deviations; Q peer discipline (lines 1649–1709) instead requires distinct conditional beliefs \(\beta_i[t_i]\neq\beta_i[\hat t_i]\), explicit quadratic peer scores, utility cancellation, and potentially unbounded off-path penalties. P sec. 3 and Appendix prompts (lines 181–244, 1046–1121) provide a cheap-talk reviewer–critic exchange, no type reports, known belief map, or reward. A critic is not Q’s peer-scoring instrument merely by being another model. I will test a narrower evidence-verification/oversight connection.

Q’s peer-discipline Proposition (Q.tex, “Peer discipline,” lines 1650–1738) assumes finite supported private types, distinct peer-report beliefs \(\beta_i[t_i]\ne\beta_i[\hat t_i]\), simultaneous type reports, and a large enforceable score \(\Lambda[2\beta_i[\hat t_i](\hat t_{-i})-\|\beta_i[\hat t_i]\|_2^2]\) plus action-support penalties and utility cancellation. P’s AR critic instead reads R’s latest review and exchange before saying AGREE/DISAGREE (P.tex, lines 193–204, 1083–1120), with no transfer or enforcement. Therefore nested cyclical monotonicity or Q’s peer-scoring proposition cannot be applied directly to P’s prompt-only failure. The scan’s claimed theorem-to-failure derivation is unsupported.

Sharper bridge: Q’s verification order is hard evidence, a certificate can be withheld but not counterfeited (Q.tex lines 299–308). P’s revised AR requires code citations for DISAGREE_EVIDENCE and requires R to cite code confirming/refuting a DISAGREE_CONCERN (P.tex lines 338–356, 1122–1235). But a code citation verifies only that text exists, not that a semantic bug is real; for omitted behavior or repo-context bugs, a diff-local witness may not exist. Hypothesis: evidence-gated disagreement improves locally falsifiable flags yet may suppress valid non-local concerns. Test by annotating bug witnesses (diff-local versus requires spec/repo/test) and measuring critic→reviewer reversals and final false negatives, with a blind first judgment/control. This is a prediction neither paper establishes, and Q’s hard-evidence assumption marks exactly where transfer can fail.

Sharper cross-paper question: does allowing C to see R’s review before C makes any independent commitment destroy the peer-information Q needs? In Q’s peer-score proof the distribution of peer reports conditional on R’s private type is treated as exogenous to R’s own report; in P, C explicitly conditions on R’s review (P.tex lines 1083–1120, 1185–1235), and Case B shows C yielding to R’s unsupported rebuttal (lines 328–337). Proposed hybrid: C first records a blind, immutable bug/no-bug judgment and code citations on the frozen diff; only then sees R’s review and audits it. Randomize baseline AR, text-constrained AR, and blind-commit-plus-interaction on the same PRs. Measure initial-to-final dissent survival and externally adjudicated bug precision/recall, stratified by whether blind R/C signals differ. This preserves P’s interactive loop while making the independent signal needed for Q-style peer scoring observable. A proper scoring extension would require enforceable rewards and calibrated conditional peer-report laws, so it is a separate treatment, not something P already supplies.

Concrete boundary/counterexample to naively importing Q’s peer score into P: take two private types \(A,B\) with calibrated peer laws \(\beta_A=(0.9,0.1)\), \(\beta_B=(0.4,0.6)\) over peer reports \((A,B)\). Q’s quadratic score is \(q(r,z)=2\beta_r(z)-\|\beta_r\|_2^2\), giving \(q(A,A)=0.98\) and \(q(B,B)=0.68\). If the peer copies the first agent’s public report (the extreme of P-like conversational dependence), a true \(B\)-type earns \(0.98\) by reporting \(A\), versus \(0.68\) truthfully, even though Q’s separation \(\beta_A\ne\beta_B\) holds. These conditionals are jointly feasible (exchangeable masses proportional to \(P(A,A):P(A,B):P(B,A):P(B,B)=9:1:1:1.5\)). This does not refute Q: its peer distribution is exogenous under unilateral misreports, whereas copying makes it endogenous. It predicts that adding peer-score rewards to an uncommitted sequential critic could worsen false consensus. Blind, sealed initial peer reports restore the key exogeneity condition for a subsequent score; interaction may proceed afterward.

My preferred publishable question is now narrower than the scan’s: when does interactive auditing consume independent peer information, and can a sealed initial critic commitment preserve it without losing P’s later critique? Q’s score proof yields a precise negative control: distinct private signals alone are insufficient once peer reports respond to the agent being scored (Q.tex, “Peer discipline,” lines 1650–1738; counterexample in ledger #7). P supplies the failure setting, especially C yielding after R’s unsupported response in Case B (P.tex lines 328–337), but does not establish this causal mechanism. A paired randomized experiment should cross blind initial C commitment (yes/no) with P’s three-way evidence prompt (yes/no), keep model/context/token budget fixed, and adjudicate bug-level precision, recall, dissent survival, and final patch success. The interaction term asks whether evidence text alone works when C’s independent signal has already been overwritten. A null benefit of commitment, or unchanged false-consensus rates despite preserved initial dissent, would falsify the proposed informational mechanism. Q’s hard-evidence order also does not follow from P’s line citations: cited code can be semantically irrelevant (ledger #5); stratify diff-local versus repo/spec-dependent bugs. This is a theory-motivated empirical proposal, not an existing theorem about LLM prompts. Remaining unknowns: whether R/C initial judgments have enough conditional separation, whether copying is substantial beyond the two cases, and whether cost-normalized gains survive.

I wrote emmy/verification_boundary.md with a scoped claim and experiment. Cross-check of Ada’s #6: a sealed blind C judgment would make pre-exposure information observable and remove R→C conversational influence at that stage, but it still does not establish Q’s separation condition \(\beta_i[t_i]\neq\beta_i[\hat t_i]\) or the enforceable scores/off-path penalties of Q prop. “Peer scoring” must remain a separate, stronger treatment. My distinct proposed test is witness-class interaction: strict diff-citation gates may improve precision for diff-local bugs while losing true concerns requiring spec/repo/test evidence; an explicit unresolved-and-query state could recover them. Q’s verification order supplies the boundary because a code quote is not a non-counterfeitable certificate of semantic correctness.

Cross-checked Ada #7–8: the quadratic scores are \(q(A,A)=2(0.9)-(0.9^2+0.1^2)=0.98\) and \(q(B,B)=2(0.6)-(0.4^2+0.6^2)=0.68\); the stated joint masses imply the conditional peer laws, so public-report copying defeats truthful scoring without contradicting Q. This is a stronger formal bridge than my certificate-only information lemma. I support a factorial test of blind commitment and evidence prompts, with my witness-location stratification. Caveat: sealing C’s first report restores exogeneity relative to R’s report, not truthful reporting or Q’s full mechanism; shared model errors can still erase informational separation. The two lines are complementary rather than contradictory.

Cross-check of Emmy #10: P’s three-way DISAGREE_CONCERN is defined as doubt about an existing reviewer flag that lacks contradicting code; R must then cite diff code to confirm or refute that flag (P.tex lines 342–356, 1151–1173, 1215–1232). The critic is separately told to name missed real bugs, and R is told to incorporate a missed bug under any verdict (P.tex lines 1207–1214, 1174–1175). Thus a strict diff-citation gate directly targets challenged existing flags; suppression of valid missed bugs requiring external context is a plausible downstream effect, not the literal rule. Any witness-class experiment should distinguish challenged flags, new missed-bug suggestions, and final formatter effects. I agree with Emmy’s core point that a cited line is not Q’s hard certificate of semantic correctness.

Current synthesis after Emmy #11 and correction #13: The promising paper is a causal study of information loss in reviewer–critic protocols, with a small formal boundary. Q’s peer-score gain \,\(\Lambda\|\beta_i[t_i]-\beta_i[\hat t_i]\|_2^2\) assumes a co-player report law unaffected by i’s report (Q.tex lines 1650–1724). P lets C see R’s review and later rebuttal before final AGREE (P.tex lines 1083–1121, 328–337); thus conversational dependence is a concrete mechanism by which Q’s proof premise can fail, though P’s two cases do not establish it as the dominant cause. The copycat calculation in #7 is a counterexample to a naive scoring transplant. Compare ordinary AR against blind sealed first-pass C, crossed with original versus three-way evidence prompts. Observe C’s initial signal, revision, final review, bug-level precision/recall and test outcome, with equal budget; classify challenged existing flags separately from newly proposed missed bugs, and diff-local versus context-dependent witnesses (Emmy #10; correction #13). The first-pass seal tests whether preserving independent information reduces false consensus; witness class tests when citation requirements help. If sealed dissent persists but accuracy does not improve, independent-information loss alone is insufficient. This is a publication candidate contingent on empirical effect and cost; neither theorem nor P’s aggregate F1 currently proves it. Unresolved: conditional signal separation, causality of copying beyond case B, citation semantics, and reproducibility of gains.

Ada #13 is right: I overstated the direct scope of P’s code-citation gate. P lines 342–356 and 1151–1173 require a diff citation when R responds to C’s DISAGREE_CONCERN about an existing R flag; P lines 1207–1214 and 1172–1175 separately ask C to name missed bugs and R to incorporate them under any verdict. I revised emmy/verification_boundary.md accordingly. The direct witness-class prediction now concerns challenged existing flags; effects on new missed-bug suggestions and final formatting are separate causal paths. The observation-equivalence argument still applies to any review decision restricted to visible evidence, but it is not evidence that P’s actual prompt suppresses missed bugs.
